Received 18 July 2024 l Revised 2 January 2025 l Accepted 16 January 2025 l Published online 22 May 2025 Abstract: Objective: Hibiscus rosa-sinensis and Centella asiatica are medicinal plants used as an alternative therapy for wound healing, and many studies have reported evidence of their effectiveness in treating wounds. This study aimed to evaluate the histological and molecular changes observed in the healing properties of a Hibiscus rosa-sinensis and Centella asiatica extracts combination (HRSCA) on wounds. Material and Methods: Twenty-four rats were randomly divided into 4 groups (untreated, 10% Povidone-Iodine solution; 5.0% and 10.0% HRSCA). The excisional wounds were inflicted using a tissue biopsy punch and treated once daily for 14 days. The wound healing properties and tensile strength test were measured. A 3D organotypic skin model using human keratinocytes and human dermal fibroblast cell lines in a collagen type 1 scaffold was developed to further evaluate the wound healing properties. Full-thickness wound was induced and was either treated with 5% HRSCA or left untreated. qRT-PCR was used to evaluate the affected genes involved in the wound healing pathway. Results: The in vivo model showed no significant differences in tensile strength between groups. However, HRSCA treatment significantly enhanced wound healing. The 3D assay revealed HRSCA modulated genes like COL53A, CSF2, CXCL11, CXCL5, IL6ST, ITGA5, PLAT, and WISP1. Conclusion: HRSCA enhanced wound closure in in vivo and 3D organotypic skin models, potentially through several pathways, such as inflammatory as well as extracellular matrix and adhesion pathways. The findings from this study provide substantial evidence regarding the wound healing potential of HRSCA. JSON: Name: hrs_ca_wound_healing_pipeline Title: Combined in vivo and 3D organotypic evaluation of Hibiscus rosa-sinensis and Centella asiatica extract combination (HRSCA) for acceleration of full-thickness cutaneous wound healing and pathway-specific molecular modulation Short Hypothesis: Topical application of a 5% Hibiscus rosa-sinensis and Centella asiatica extract combination (HRSCA) accelerates full-thickness cutaneous wound closure versus vehicle by increasing re-epithelialization rate and modulating wound-healing gene expression (including upregulation of WISP1 and downregulation of COL5A3, CXCL11, ITGA1/ITGA5) within 14 days. Related Work: Prior studies report that Hibiscus rosa-sinensis extracts improve tensile strength, epithelialization, and collagen arrangement in rodent wound models; Centella asiatica extracts (notably asiaticoside) promote collagen synthesis, antioxidant activity, angiogenesis, and faster epithelial closure in animal and cell models. Existing approaches are limited by: (1) single-plant evaluations without testing synergistic combinations; (2) reliance on 2D cell assays or small-animal endpoints without human-relevant 3D organotypic models; (3) sparse molecular profiling beyond a few markers (hydroxyproline, broad collagen content) limiting mechanistic interpretation; (4) inconsistent extract preparation, dosing, and lack of phytochemical standardization; (5) small sample sizes and single timepoint tensile strength measures that limit assessment of remodeling. No prior work systematically compares combination versus individual extracts across matched in vivo and human 3D models with multiplex transcriptomic readouts and parallel functional endpoints. Abstract: This pipeline evaluates whether a topical combination of Hibiscus rosa-sinensis and Centella asiatica extracts (HRSCA) accelerates cutaneous wound healing and identifies molecular pathways mediating effects using parallel in vivo and 3D human organotypic models. The approach integrates a randomized rodent excisional wound model with serial wound-area, re-epithelialization, histology and tensile-strength endpoints, and a human keratinocyte–fibroblast collagen-based 3D organotypic assay with punch-wound, migration, and molecular profiling (RT-qPCR panel and RNA-seq). Key comparisons include HRSCA versus vehicle, povidone-iodine, and single-plant extracts at two concentrations. The main contributions are (1) standardized experimental pipeline linking functional healing outcomes to pathway-level gene regulation and (2) direct assessment of combination synergy and dose-response in both species-relevant and human-tissue models. Expected outcomes are reproducible acceleration of wound closure, specific modulation of inflammatory, extracellular-matrix and adhesion pathways, and a prioritized set of candidate molecular targets for follow-up mechanistic studies. Experiments: In vivo rodent excision study: subjects: male Wistar rats, randomized into six groups (n=12 per group): (A) untreated vehicle, (B) vehicle+ethanol control, (C) 10% povidone-iodine (positive control), (D) 5% HRSCA, (E) 10% HRSCA, (F) single-extract controls (5% Hibiscus alone and 5% Centella alone; split into two groups of n=12 each). Sample size rationale: powered to detect 20% difference in wound area at day 14 with 80% power and α=0.05. Procedures: full-thickness 8 mm dorsal excisional wounds; topical application once daily; endpoints at days 0,2,4,6,8,10,12,14 and extended remodeling timepoints day 21 and 28. Measurements: digital planimetry wound area (% of baseline), period of re-epithelialization (day scab falls), tensile strength (g/mm2) at days 14 and 28, blinded histology scoring (granulation tissue, inflammatory infiltrate, collagen maturity via Masson's trichrome) and immunohistochemistry for CD31 (angiogenesis) and α-SMA (myofibroblasts). 3D organotypic human skin model: HaCaT keratinocytes co-cultured with human dermal fibroblasts in type I collagen scaffold; groups: unwounded, wounded+vehicle, wounded+5% HRSCA, wounded+5% Hibiscus, wounded+5% Centella (biological replicates n=5 per group). Procedures: full-thickness punch wound in construct, topical treatment daily, sample collection at 0, 16, 24, 72, and 336 hours. Measurements: punch-migration area, histology for stratification and collagen deposition, live/dead and cytotoxicity assays, and qRT-PCR panel (84 wound-healing genes) plus RNA-seq (transcriptome) at 24h and 14 days. Baselines and comparisons: compare combination vs. vehicle, positive control (povidone-iodine for in vivo), and each single-extract control. Ablation/contrast studies: dose-response (5% vs 10% HRSCA), combination vs each single extract, 3D vs 2D monoculture migration assays. Metrics and statistics: primary metric wound area reduction (%) at day 14; secondary metrics period of re-epithelialization, tensile strength, histology scores, migration rate (mm2/h), differential gene expression (log2 fold-change, adjusted p<0.05). Statistical tests: mixed-effects repeated-measures ANOVA for time-series, Tukey post-hoc for pairwise group comparisons, Benjamini-Hochberg correction for transcriptomics. Data quality controls: phytochemical batch profiling (HPLC), endotoxin assay, blinding of outcome assessors, technical triplicates for molecular assays. Risk Factors and Limitations: Extract variability and standardization: botanical extracts contain variable phytochemical profiles across batches, affecting reproducibility and dose equivalence. Translatability: rodent skin and simplified 3D organotypic constructs lack full immune complexity and vascularization of human wounds; molecular signals may not predict clinical outcomes. Attribution: transcriptomic correlation does not prove causal mechanisms; observed gene changes may be secondary. Sample size and statistical power: effect sizes smaller than anticipated may yield underpowered comparisons, especially in transcriptomics. Measurement bias: planimetry and histology scoring require strict blinding to avoid observer bias. Toxicity and off-target effects: complex extracts may elicit uncharacterized local or systemic toxicity not captured in short-term studies. Scalability and regulatory: extract manufacturing at clinical grade and consistent supply chains may limit translation. Computational/bioinformatic risks: batch effects, multiple testing, and false discovery in RNA-seq may confound interpretation. Time-scale limits: short-term endpoints (≤28 days) may miss long-term remodeling, scarring, or recurrence outcomes.
